title: Mata v. Avianca, Inc. — June 22, 2023 Sanctions Decision
lead: Lawyers opposing dismissal submit nonexistent cases generated by ChatGPT and continue relying on them after the opponent and court cannot locate them. The sanctions inquiry focuses on each lawyer’s investigation, sworn statements, and conduct after those warnings.

actors.name: Roberto Mata
actors.role: Passenger alleging a knee injury from an airline serving cart.

actors.name: Avianca, Inc.
actors.role: Airline asserting a Montreal Convention limitations defense.

actors.name: Steven Schwartz
actors.role: Lawyer performing research and drafting while not admitted in the federal district.

actors.name: Peter LoDuca
actors.role: Federal counsel who signed the challenged submissions.

actors.name: Levidow, Levidow & Oberman
actors.role: Law firm held jointly responsible with both lawyers.

actors.name: Judge P. Kevin Castel
actors.role: District judge deciding the court-initiated sanctions proceeding.

proceedings: Avianca removed the passenger’s state action and moved to dismiss as untimely.
After fabricated authorities were submitted and then furnished as purported opinions, the court issued show-cause orders and held a hearing.
The court imposed a single joint $5,000 penalty and required notice letters with specified documents, without resolving the underlying injury claim in this order.
limits: This account transforms the canonical sanctions brief without a fresh audit or later-history review. Purported case texts are evidence of fabrication, not authorities. The order applied the Second Circuit’s subjective-bad-faith standard for this court-initiated inquiry. It was neither a criminal forgery conviction nor a decision of the substantive injury or limitations merits.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A removed airline case requires federal legal research
sections.cue: Who prepared and who signed the opposition?
paragraphs: In February 2022, Roberto Mata sued Avianca in New York state court, alleging a metal serving cart struck his left knee on a flight from El Salvador to John F. Kennedy Airport. Avianca removed on federal-question grounds under the Montreal Convention and later sought dismissal under that treaty’s limitations period.

Steven Schwartz of Levidow, Levidow & Oberman had handled the state case but was not admitted in the Southern District of New York. Colleague Peter LoDuca appeared there while Schwartz continued substantive work. After encountering limited federal access through the firm’s Fastcase subscription, Schwartz treated ChatGPT as a search engine and requested cases supporting tolling during a bankruptcy stay. He used its excerpts without obtaining full decisions. Apart from an unsuccessful initial search and limited authentication, it supplied the substantive arguments.

On March 1, 2023, LoDuca signed and filed Schwartz’s opposition affirmation with a declaration under penalty of perjury. He reviewed flow and grammar but read no cited decision and made no inquiry into its legal basis. He relied on a colleague of more than twenty-five years despite Schwartz’s primarily state-court practice and lack of experience with these federal issues.

sections.title: Warnings lead to another unverified sworn submission
sections.cue: What did the lawyers do when the cases could not be found?
paragraphs: Avianca’s March 15 reply identified several unlocatable decisions and said the real cases did not support the asserted propositions. LoDuca forwarded it without reading it; no respondent withdrew or explained the submission. The court’s own searches also failed.

Orders on April 11 and 12 required actual opinions. LoDuca obtained an extension by falsely saying he was on vacation when Schwartz was away. The court later found that statement concealed Schwartz’s substantive role and LoDuca’s lack of verification.

On April 25, LoDuca signed an affidavit Schwartz prepared, attaching purported case excerpts. It said one authority could not be found and attributed incomplete texts to an unspecified online database, without naming ChatGPT. LoDuca had not prepared it, did not know whether its assertions were true, and asked no questions or checked the cases before signing.

sections.title: The purported decisions reveal fabrication, and the court opens sanctions proceedings
sections.cue: Why were these more than citation errors?
paragraphs: The attached Varghese, Miller, Petersen, Shaboon, Martinez, and Durden opinions did not exist; ChatGPT generated them. Varghese borrowed identifiers from unrelated cases, changed plaintiffs and bankruptcy chapters, included unrelated passages, cited fabricated or misdescribed authority, and ended abruptly. Miller used unrelated docket and reporter locations and falsely attributed authorship to a panel. Petersen mismatched identifiers, confused jurisdictions, and cited itself. Names of actual judges and litigants supplied superficial credibility while falsely implicating them.

A May 4 show-cause order addressed LoDuca’s opposition and attachments. The May 25 response first admitted their fictitious origin. A May 26 supplemental order added Schwartz and the firm and addressed notarization. With separate counsel and further declarations, the respondents attended a June 8 hearing; both lawyers answered under oath and expressed remorse.

Schwartz’s accounts changed. May 25 screenshots of ChatGPT assurances that cases were real suggested those assurances explained his earlier reliance. His June 6 declaration instead described post-show-cause queries as confirming an emerging belief that the system answered without regard to truth. The court found those explanations inconsistent. It rejected claimed ignorance of possible fabrication until May 4 because Schwartz had read Avianca’s challenge, knew the court could not locate cases, and unsuccessfully searched for Varghese and the cited Zicherman authority himself. No respondent ever formally withdrew the original affirmation or told the court to disregard it.

sections.title: Established duties govern both filing and later advocacy
sections.cue: Why did this inquiry require subjective bad faith?
paragraphs: Judge P. Kevin Castel recognized that assistance from reliable technology, people, or databases was not inherently improper. Lawyers nevertheless remained responsible for accuracy. Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11(b)(2) required reasonable inquiry supporting legal contentions in existing law or a nonfrivolous proposal to change it. Mistakes and weak theories were not automatically sanctionable, but invented opinions were neither law nor a legitimate basis for legal development.

The rule covered signing, filing, submitting, and later advocating. Failure to correct after discovering unsupported contentions could constitute continued advocacy. Rule 11(c)(3) allowed a specifically described court-initiated inquiry after notice and an opportunity to respond. Responsibility could reach Schwartz despite his neither signing nor appearing, and the firm was jointly responsible absent exceptional circumstances.

Under the Second Circuit precedent governing this court-initiated process, subjective bad faith was required, a higher standard than objective unreasonableness ordinarily associated with an adversary’s motion and twenty-one-day safe harbor. Inherent-authority sanctions also required bad faith and restraint. Knowing falsehood or conscious avoidance of a recognized high probability could qualify; negligence, confusion, foolishness, or sloppy research alone could not.

sources.pinpoint: ECF 54, introduction pp.1–3; Conclusions of Law ¶¶ 1–5, 9–19, pp.21–28

sections.title: The court makes separate bad-faith findings for each lawyer
sections.cue: What conduct exceeded an imperfect investigation?
paragraphs: The court distinguished Braun v. Zhiguo Fu, where innocent reliance on another person gave the lawyer no reason to suspect falsehood. Here explicit opponent and judicial warnings required inquiry. LoDuca avoided reading the challenge, checked no case, and ignored known limits on Schwartz’s experience and research resources. He then swore to assertions without any basis. A cursory substantive review would have exposed missing and internally inconsistent material; his knowingly false vacation statement independently supported bad faith.

For Schwartz, failed searches, Avianca’s warning, and the court’s orders established awareness of a high probability of fabrication. He supplied the purported opinions without disclosing failed searches and consciously avoided confirmation. Misleadingly calling ChatGPT merely supplemental, giving inconsistent authenticity-query accounts, and omitting its role from the April affidavit strengthened the finding.

The firm accepted responsibility and identified corrections but showed no exceptional circumstances excusing Rule 11(c)(1) joint responsibility. It was jointly and severally responsible with both lawyers.

sections.title: The judge limits both the sanctioning grounds and the remedy
sections.cue: What exactly had to be paid and sent?
paragraphs: The court declined an independent sanction under 28 U.S.C. § 1927 because it had not found dilatory tactics or delay of the kind addressed by unreasonable and vexatious multiplication. Rule 11 and, alternatively, inherent authority supplied the grounds. Discussion of 18 U.S.C. § 505 illustrated the concern with counterfeit judicial authority, but no forged signature or seal appeared, so the respondents had not violated that criminal statute.

Deterrence governed selection. Planned firm education on technology, artificial intelligence, and notarization made additional court-ordered education redundant. Avianca requested no fees or expenses, and none were awarded. Remorse, embarrassment, clean disciplinary histories, absence of financial gain or personal animus, and low repetition risk mitigated consequences without negating violations.

On June 22, 2023, the court imposed one $5,000 penalty, jointly and severally payable by LoDuca, Schwartz, and the firm to the court registry within fourteen days—not $5,000 each or compensation to Avianca. Within the same period, respondents had to send individually addressed first-class letters to Mata enclosing the opinion, June 8 transcript, and April 25 submission with exhibits. They also had to send corresponding letters to every judge falsely identified as author of the six opinions, including the purported opinion attributed to that judge, and file copies of the letters.

The court declined to compel apologies because involuntary apologies would lack sincerity; notice and documents were mandatory, apologies voluntary. Castel alone issued the order, with no appellate voting alignment or separate opinion. It resolved sanctions rather than Mata’s substantive claim or the merits of Avianca’s limitations defense.
